evidenceHint.en: Dataset resource catalogue giving, per system, every set's origin, permitting agreement, storage location and consuming systems

text.en: List the training, tuning, evaluation and reference datasets per system.
Record where each dataset came from and who supplied or generated it.
Attach the licence, contract or consent basis permitting the intended use.
Note where the working copy is held and which systems read from it.
Flag datasets whose permission to use is time-limited or already expired.

title.en: Register the models, algorithms and computing environments each AI system runs on

description.en: A system in production is an artefact at a version, assembled from libraries at versions, served on infrastructure somebody pays for, and none of that is recoverable after the fact if nobody wrote it down. Capture per system the model or algorithm and its version, whether it was built in-house, purchased or taken from an open-source repository, the frameworks, libraries and external inference APIs it calls, and the environments it is trained and served in, naming provider, region, accelerator class and the account holder. Without it a vulnerable library, an expiring reservation or a withdrawn hosted model cannot be traced to the systems it takes down.

evidenceHint.en: Technical resource register linking every model artefact, library dependency, external API and hosting environment to the system using it

text.en: List each model or algorithm in use with its version and build date.
Mark each as built in-house, purchased, or taken from open source.
List the frameworks, libraries and external inference APIs each system calls.
Record the training environment: provider, region and accelerator class.
Record the serving environment and who owns the account paying for it.
Link every entry back to the system record it belongs to.

title.en: Update the named holders and competences on every resource record, and flag the sole-holder duties

description.en: People move on, change teams and take specialist knowledge with them, so the human half of a resource record decays faster than its hardware or its data. Each cycle, walk the duties recorded for building, deploying, monitoring and overseeing the AI work: confirm the named holder is still in post and still doing that job, attach the training, certification or supervised practice that supports the competence claimed, and strike out anyone who has left. Where exactly one qualified person can carry a duty, record it as a concentration risk together with a deputy or a date by which cover will exist. Skip the pass and the record keeps showing a staffing picture that quietly stopped being true, and a single resignation takes out a capability nobody knew rested on one desk.

evidenceHint.en: Competence and cover review for the period: one row per duty giving its named holder, the evidence of current competence, the date checked, and for a sole-holder duty the agreed deputy or cover date

text.en: Pull the current holder list from HR and the access directory for every duty on the record.
Confirm each named holder is still in post and still carrying that duty.
Attach the training, certification or supervised practice that evidences present competence.
Mark any duty that exactly one qualified person can carry as a concentration risk.
Agree a deputy or a cross-training date for every duty marked, and record it.

title.en: Reconcile the resource records against the models, data stores and compute actually running

description.en: A resource register decays quietly: a model is swapped at a release, a dataset is re-pointed, training moves region for cost, a team reorganises, and nothing in the record says so. Once in the period take evidence from the systems themselves, from deployment manifests, model registries, storage and cloud billing accounts and access logs, and compare it with what the records claim. Two findings matter: entries describing something that is no longer there, and running AI for which no record was ever opened, which the register can never reveal from the inside. Correct each record and name the change route that bypassed it.

evidenceHint.en: Reconciliation report comparing register entries with deployed artefacts and accounts, listing unrecorded systems and the corrections applied

text.en: Export what is deployed from manifests, model registries and cloud accounts.
Compare each running artefact and environment with its register entry.
List entries with no counterpart and workloads with no register entry.
Correct the affected records and date every correction applied.
Identify the change route that let an unrecorded system reach production.

templates.title: A.5 Assessing impacts of AI systems
templates.description: Implements AIMS-10: A.5 Assessing impacts of AI systems — a repeatable process for judging what each AI system does to the individuals who meet it, to the groups it treats as a class, and to society at large, together with the records that process leaves behind. Covers naming the affected parties for every system, the procedure and the events that trigger it, a societal-impact section with its dimensions named, completed impact records broken out per affected group, and a comparison of what was predicted against what the deployed systems actually produced.

title.en: Map each AI system to the individuals, groups and communities its outputs reach

description.en: Impact assessment begins by naming who is on the receiving end, and the most exposed people are rarely the users: the applicant refused a loan, the patient a model triages, the neighbourhood a deployment concentrates in. For every AI system on the inventory, write down the individuals who interact with it, the groups whose members it treats as a class rather than one by one, and the wider communities affected by its operation although they never touch it. Note which of those parties the organisation can actually reach for comment and which it cannot, because an assessment that hears only from users will report only the impacts users can see. Attach the mapping, dated.

evidenceHint.en: Affected-party mapping giving, per system, the people who interact with it, the classes it sorts them into, and the communities downstream of its operation

text.en: Take each AI system on the resources inventory in turn.
List the individuals who interact with the system directly.
Name the groups the system treats as a class, not one by one.
Add the communities affected without ever using the system.
Mark which affected parties can be consulted and which cannot.

title.en: Assemble the impact-assessment procedure so two assessors reach the same conclusion

description.en: A process that gives a different answer depending on who runs it is not repeatable, and repeatability is what this requirement is about. Turn the organisation's assessment criteria into a procedure a project team can run without a specialist sitting beside them: the events that make it mandatory, the questions asked, the wording each severity rating must match, who has to take part, and the record template that comes out at the end. State the triggers explicitly — before a system is deployed, when a model changes materially, when it is pointed at a new population, and at a fixed interval after that — because an assessment with no trigger happens once and then never again. Attach the procedure and the blank record template.

evidenceHint.en: Impact-assessment procedure showing its trigger events, the rating wording assessors must use, and the blank record template it produces

text.en: Set the events that make an impact assessment mandatory.
Draft the question set a project team can answer unaided.
Fix the wording each severity rating has to match.
Name who must take part, including an affected-party voice.
Publish the blank record template the procedure fills in.

title.en: Extend the assessment to societal effects that no individual would think to report

description.en: Harm to a person arrives as a complaint; harm to society arrives as nothing at all, so the method has to go looking for it. Add a societal section that considers by name the dimensions this organisation's systems can actually move — employment and de-skilling in the roles being automated, access to essential services for people who cannot use the system, the environmental load of training and serving it, the effect on public information where outputs are published, and the concentration of decisions in a single model. Require a written reason whenever a dimension is judged not applicable, because a blank section and a considered 'not relevant here' look identical a year later. Attach the societal section with the sources consulted for it.

evidenceHint.en: Societal-impact section of the method, naming every dimension considered, the evidence source used for each, and the reasons recorded for those ruled out

text.en: Name the societal dimensions the assessment must cover.
State where the evidence for each dimension comes from.
Require a recorded reason when a dimension is ruled out.
Test the section against one system already in service.

title.en: File a dated impact record for each assessment, split by the groups affected

description.en: Run the procedure when its triggers fire and keep what comes out as a record rather than a slide that disappears with the meeting. Each record names the system and version assessed, the date, who took part, the individuals, groups and communities carried over from the mapping, the effect found for each of them with its rating, the societal findings, the mitigations chosen and those rejected with the reason, and the residual impact accepted with the name of whoever accepted it. An effect written down only as one overall rating hides the case this control exists for: a system that is fine on average and severe for one group. Attach the records completed in the period alongside the list of triggers that fired.

evidenceHint.en: Completed impact records for the period, each showing the effect rated per affected party, the societal findings, and who accepted the residual impact

text.en: Open a record as soon as a trigger fires, before deployment.
Carry the affected parties across from the system mapping.
Rate the effect found for each group separately, not in total.
Write down mitigations chosen and those rejected, with reasons.
Name who accepted any residual impact and date the acceptance.

title.en: Compare predicted impacts against the outcomes the deployed systems actually produced

description.en: An impact assessment is a forecast, and a forecast nobody checks back on is indistinguishable from a guess. Take the records covering the period and set each predicted effect beside what the organisation can observe: complaints and appeals received, refusal and error rates broken out by the groups the mapping named, anything arriving through the external reporting channel, and what people outside the organisation have said about the system. Where an outcome is worse than predicted, or a group judged unaffected turns up in the complaints, reopen the assessment instead of quietly amending its rating, and date the reassessment. Attach the comparison together with the list of records reopened.

evidenceHint.en: Prediction-versus-outcome comparison for the period, naming the assessments reopened and the parties whose observed treatment differed from the forecast

text.en: Pull the impact records that covered the period under review.
Set each predicted effect beside its observed outcome.
Break complaints and error rates out by affected group.
Reopen any assessment whose outcome was worse than predicted.
Send the comparison into the next management review.

templates.title: A.6 AI system life cycle
templates.description: Implements AIMS-11: the responsible development objectives and documented build process, per-system functional and non-functional requirements with their design record, the verification and validation methodology and the release criteria that gate a deployment, and the life-cycle event log that shows which model version went live, on whose authority and with what documentation handed over.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Head of AI Engineering / Engineering Lead

title.en: Express the responsible development objectives and the documented process every AI build follows

description.en: Turn the organisation's responsible-AI aims into properties a build can be checked against — accuracy floors, robustness on degraded input, explainability, the points where a person stays in the loop, the behaviour expected when the system is unsure — and set out the stages a build passes through from concept to retirement, with who signs the exit of each one. An objective stated as an aspiration cannot fail a build, and an undocumented process still exists but exists as habit: it varies by team and cannot be shown to an auditor. Both halves are the guidance every later task in this control is measured against.

evidenceHint.en: Dated development guidance giving each objective its measurable property and threshold, the stages a build passes, and the named signer closing each stage

text.en: Name the AI systems in development or planned for the coming period.
Turn each responsible-AI aim into a property a build can be measured on.
Set the threshold or target that counts as meeting each property.
Set out the stages a build passes from concept through to retirement.
Name who signs the exit of each stage and what they attest to.
Publish the guidance to every team that builds or trains AI systems.

title.en: Capture each AI system's functional and non-functional requirements and the design decisions behind them

description.en: For every system being built, write the requirements down in a form somebody can test: what it must do, and the non-functional side — accuracy and error tolerance, latency, behaviour on inputs outside the training range, security, and the oversight a person must be able to exercise. Alongside them keep the design record: the model approach chosen, the alternatives rejected and why, and the constraints that shaped it, updated when the design moves rather than reconstructed from memory a year later. Requirements held only in tickets and conversation are the ones quietly dropped mid-project, and nobody can say afterwards that they were.

evidenceHint.en: Per-system specification pairing every required behaviour and quality attribute with its design rationale, versioned and dated at each revision

text.en: Collect the functional behaviour each system is required to deliver.
Add the quality attributes: accuracy, robustness, latency, security, oversight.
State each requirement so a result can be read as pass or fail.
Record the model approach chosen and the alternatives turned down.
Version the specification and note who agreed it and when.
Revise the design record whenever the approach changes during the build.

title.en: Set the verification and validation methodology and the release criteria a build must clear

description.en: Decide, before a release is in flight, how a candidate is tested and what it must reach to be let out: which evaluation data is used and why it reflects live conditions, which tests are repeated after retraining, the thresholds that block a go-live, and who may approve an exception and on what record. The deployment plan then says how the system reaches production — staged rollout, fallback, and the performance measures watched afterwards with the people who watch them. Criteria settled while a release is in flight are always the criteria that candidate happens to meet.

evidenceHint.en: Test and deployment plan naming the evaluations run, the thresholds that block a go-live, the rollout and fallback steps, and the post-release measures with their watchers

text.en: Choose the evaluation data and say why it reflects live conditions.
List the tests repeated after retraining or a material change.
Fix the thresholds below which a candidate cannot be released.
Name who may approve an exception and what they must write down.
Set the rollout, fallback and post-deployment monitoring arrangements.

title.en: Log each AI release, model version and retirement as it happens through the period

description.en: Keep one running record of life-cycle events — training runs, evaluations, go-lives, material configuration changes, withdrawals and retirements — each with its date, version, authorising person and the evidence that the release criteria were cleared. Attach the technical documentation handed to the people who run the system, matched to the version actually deployed rather than the one the pack was first written for. Assembled after the fact this log is a best guess; kept as events happen it is the only way to answer which model was live on a given day and what was known about it then.

evidenceHint.en: Life-cycle event export covering the period, one entry per training run, go-live, change and withdrawal, each linked to its clearance evidence and the handover pack issued

text.en: Record an entry for every training run, release, change and retirement.
Give each entry its date, version identifier and authorising person.
Link each release entry to the evidence that cleared its criteria.
Attach the technical documentation issued for the deployed version.
Note the monitoring switched on at go-live and who receives its output.
Export the log at period end and hold it as the period's evidence.

title.en: Trace a deployed AI system back through its verification results to the requirements it was built on

description.en: Take a system that went live during the period and follow it backwards: every requirement to the result that verified it, the design record to the version actually running, and the documentation its operators hold to the version they are operating. This is where life-cycle paperwork fails in practice — a requirement dropped quietly during development, a test run against a model two versions old, a handover pack describing behaviour that changed at the last release. Record each mismatch with the correction agreed and the person who owns it, and feed anything systemic back into the development guidance.

evidenceHint.en: Traceability review record naming the system sampled, every mismatch found between what was required, tested, built and handed over, and the fix agreed with its owner

text.en: Pick a system that went live during the period as the sample.
Match every stated requirement to the result that verified it.
Check the design record describes the version actually running.
Confirm operators hold documentation for the version they run.
Record each mismatch, the correction agreed and who owns it.

templates.title: A.7 Data for AI systems
templates.description: Implements AIMS-12: A.7 Data for AI systems — where each dataset used to build or retrain a model came from and why it was chosen, the quality criteria it must clear and the evidence it cleared them, the preparation applied between the raw source and the training set, and the lineage joining a deployed model back to the records behind it.

title.en: Trace each dataset back to the source it came from and the reason it was chosen

description.en: For every dataset feeding development, retraining or evaluation, follow it back to where it actually originated — a supplier feed, a customer-data extract, a public corpus, a synthetic generator — and record who provided it, under what licence, contract or consent basis, and what uses those terms permit. Second-hand data is what bites: a corpus a supplier assembled from sources they will not name cannot be defended to an auditor or a regulator, and the moment to discover that is before it trains anything. Record alongside it why this data was selected and what was rejected, since a selection nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from whatever was easiest to obtain.

evidenceHint.en: Provenance entry per dataset naming the supplier, acquisition route, licence or consent basis, permitted uses and the selection reasoning

text.en: List every dataset that feeds a model in development, retraining or evaluation.
Follow each one back to the supplier, extract or feed that produced it.
Record the licence, contract or consent basis that permits the intended use.
State why this data was selected and which alternatives were rejected.
Flag any dataset whose origin cannot be established and route it to legal review.

title.en: Set the quality thresholds a dataset must clear before it trains anything

description.en: Write down, per dataset and for the purpose it serves, what good enough means in numbers: completeness, label accuracy, duplication, class balance, how current the records are, and coverage of the populations the system will actually be used on. Criteria stated as adjectives cannot be verified — 'representative' passes whatever dataset somebody already wanted to use — so each one needs a measurement method, a threshold and a stated consequence when data arrives below it. Agree them with the people who have to meet them, or the thresholds get quietly reinterpreted at the first deadline.

evidenceHint.en: Data-quality criteria sheet giving every measure a method, a numeric bar and the action required when data falls under it

text.en: Name the quality dimensions that matter for each dataset's purpose.
Give every dimension a measurement method and a numeric threshold.
State the coverage required for the populations the system will affect.
Say what happens when a dataset arrives below one of the thresholds.
Agree the criteria with the model owner who has to meet them.

title.en: Capture every preparation step that turns the raw source into a training set

description.en: Describe the pipeline between the data as it arrived and the data the model actually sees: cleaning and de-duplication, filtering and exclusion rules, labelling and whoever or whatever applied the labels, feature engineering, normalisation, augmentation, any synthetic records added, and how the training, validation and test split was drawn. Preparation is where silent damage happens — an exclusion rule that drops a whole population, an augmentation that multiplies one class — and none of it is visible from the raw data or from the final accuracy figure. Parameters belong in the record too: the same step at a different threshold is a different dataset.

evidenceHint.en: Per-dataset preparation description covering cleaning, exclusions, labelling method, feature handling, augmentation, synthetic content and the split

text.en: Write the ordered pipeline from raw source through to training set.
Record the parameters and thresholds each transformation ran with.
Name who or what produced the labels and how disagreements were settled.
Record every exclusion rule and the records it removes from the set.
State how the training, validation and test split was drawn.

title.en: Log each change to a training corpus against the model build it produced

description.en: Data does not sit still: a feed refreshes, a labelling pass corrects old records, a batch is removed after a complaint, a retraining run pulls a wider window. Keep one running log in which every change carries its date, its reason, the person or job that made it, the dataset version it created and the model builds trained on that version. Without that join, a question about a deployed model's behaviour gets answered from the data currently in the bucket rather than the data the model actually saw, which is the one answer guaranteed to be wrong.

evidenceHint.en: Lineage log for the period joining dataset versions, the change that created each, and the model builds trained on them

text.en: Give every dataset version an identifier the build records can cite.
Log each refresh, correction, removal and addition with its reason.
Record the person or scheduled job that made the change, and when.
Link each model build to the exact dataset versions it consumed.
Keep superseded versions readable for as long as the model runs.

title.en: Re-verify the declared quality criteria against the data now in live use

description.en: At the review interval, re-run each defined measurement against the data that is training and evaluating models today, rather than against the snapshot measured when the criteria were written. Read the misses instead of the summary: a corpus that cleared every bar at onboarding drifts as feeds change, labels accumulate and the population shifts, and these measurements are the only thing that will say so before the model does. Take one deployed model in the same pass and walk it back through the log to the source records it trained on — a lineage that cannot be walked is a lineage that does not exist.

evidenceHint.en: Verification results per dataset: measured value against its bar, every failure with an owner and fix, plus one completed traceback

text.en: Take the datasets training or evaluating models in this period.
Re-run every defined measurement against the current contents.
Compare each measured value with the threshold it has to clear.
Pick one deployed model and trace it back to its source records.
Record each failure with an owner and the correction applied.

templates.title: A.8 Information for interested parties
templates.description: Implements AIMS-13: what the organisation tells the people outside it about its AI systems — user-facing documentation of purpose and limits, a working route for outsiders to report AI behaviour they consider wrong, a plan for notifying affected people when an AI system fails, and proactive disclosure when a system changes underneath them.

title.en: Determine which AI failures oblige an outward notice, to whom and within what time

description.en: Decide in advance what an AI system doing the wrong thing obliges the organisation to say publicly: which failure kinds trigger a notice (harmful output, a wrongful automated decision, behaviour outside the system's stated envelope, a data problem that changed results), which audiences each kind reaches — affected individuals, users, the wider public, a regulator — and how long the organisation gives itself before the first notice goes out. Settled during an incident instead, this becomes an argument about whether anybody needs to be told at all, while the clock runs. Attach the notification plan with its trigger-to-audience matrix and stated timings.

evidenceHint.en: Incident-notification plan: failure triggers mapped to the audiences each one reaches, the timing committed to, and the named sender

text.en: List the AI failure kinds that would warrant telling somebody outside the organisation.
Name the audiences each failure kind reaches, separating affected individuals from users.
Set the time within which the first notice leaves for each of those audiences.
Name who authorises and sends a notice, and who stands in when they are unavailable.
State what a first notice must contain while the cause is still unknown.

title.en: Publish user-facing documentation giving each AI system's purpose, limits and oversight route

description.en: Write the documentation the people who use the system, or are subject to its output, actually receive: what it is for, what it does and does not do well, the conditions under which its output degrades, what data about the person it uses, whether a human reviews its decisions and how to reach one. Documentation written for the buyer rather than the user is the common failure here — it describes capability and omits limitation, and limitation is the half that protects the reader. Attach the documentation set as published, per system.

evidenceHint.en: Published documentation set, one entry per deployed system, covering intended use, known limitations, data used and the human-contact route

text.en: List the AI systems that reach users or affected people outside the organisation.
State each system's intended purpose and the uses it is not fit for.
Describe the conditions under which its output is known to degrade.
Say what data about a person it uses and where human review applies.
Publish each entry where its audience will meet it, and date the version.

title.en: Open an outside route for reporting AI behaviour, with acknowledgement and routing rules

description.en: Stand up a channel a person outside the organisation can use to say an AI system behaved wrongly, reachable from the place the behaviour happened rather than buried in a policy page. Decide who receives the reports, what the reporter is told and how quickly, when a report escalates into the notification plan, and how somebody who is not a customer is handled — an intake that only accepts contract holders is the failure this requirement exists to prevent. Attach the channel definition with its routing and acknowledgement rules.

evidenceHint.en: Problem-intake channel definition: where it is surfaced, who triages, the response commitment and the escalation rule into incident notification

text.en: Choose the intake route and surface it where the AI system meets its audience.
Name the team that receives reports and the person accountable for triage.
Set what the reporter is told on receipt and within what period.
Write the rule that turns a report into an external notification.
Confirm somebody with no account or contract can still file a report.

title.en: Send refreshed disclosures whenever a system's purpose, data or limits change

description.en: Treat every change that moves a system away from what was published — a retrained model, a new data source, a widened purpose, a newly discovered limitation, a retirement — as a trigger to tell the audiences it affects, rather than waiting for an annual documentation refresh. The silent version of this failure is documentation that is accurate on the day it ships and describes last year's model one release later, with nobody outside able to tell. Attach the dated log of disclosures issued during the period.

evidenceHint.en: Dated communications log for the period: each triggering change, the audiences told, the notice issued and the date it went out

text.en: Take the changes released in the period that altered purpose, data or limits.
Decide for each whether the published information is now wrong or incomplete.
Issue the refreshed disclosure to the audiences the change affects.
Record the date each notice went out and who received it.
Carry the same wording into the published documentation in the same pass.

title.en: Sample the reports received and check what the reporter was told and how fast

description.en: Read the reports that actually arrived rather than the channel's own statistics: for a sample, check whether the reporter was acknowledged within the committed period, what substantive answer they got, whether the report met a notification trigger and whether the notice was in fact sent. Count the AI complaints that reached the organisation by other routes — support tickets, social media, a regulator's letter — because those are the evidence that the published channel is not reachable. Attach the review with its findings and the corrections made.

evidenceHint.en: Period review of the intake register: sampled cases with acknowledgement and resolution times, triggers met, notices issued and gaps corrected

text.en: Pull the reports logged in the period and take a sample across their kinds.
Compare each acknowledgement against the period the channel commits to.
Check whether any sampled report met a notification trigger and what followed.
Count the AI complaints that arrived through routes other than the channel.
Record each gap with an owner and the change made to close it.

templates.title: A.9 Use of AI systems
templates.description: Implements AIMS-14: keeps every AI system already in live use inside the purpose it was assessed for, through responsible-use operating processes (A.9.2), measurable objectives for systems in production (A.9.3), and an authorisation gate that catches scope creep before a deployed system is pointed at a new job (A.9.4).

title.en: Baseline the approved purpose of each AI system in live use and the uses it is not authorised for

description.en: For every AI system already running in the business, set down the purpose it was assessed and approved for, the decisions it is allowed to influence, the population it acts on, and the half that usually gets skipped: the neighbouring uses it is explicitly not authorised for. Without that second half, a later request to point the model at a different dataset looks like an ordinary feature request rather than a use nobody ever assessed. Attach the purpose baseline covering every deployed system.

evidenceHint.en: Per-system purpose baseline covering, for every system in production, its assessed use, the decisions it may influence and the uses ruled out

text.en: List every AI system currently in production use across the business.
Record the assessed purpose and the decisions each one may influence.
Name, for each system, the adjacent uses that are not authorised.
Identify the business owner who answers for how each system is used.
Have each owner confirm the baseline matches how the system is used today.

title.en: Issue operating instructions for each deployed system, including when a human must override its output

description.en: Turn the approved purpose into instructions the people who actually operate the system can follow: which inputs and requests are acceptable, what an output may not be relied on for by itself, when a human has to check or overturn it, and who to tell when it behaves oddly. Teams left without this invent their own practice, and the practice drifts further from the assessed purpose with every shortcut that happens to work. Attach the issued instructions together with proof that the using teams received them.

evidenceHint.en: Responsible-use operating procedure per system, plus the distribution record showing which teams received it and when

text.en: Set out the inputs and requests each system may be used for.
State what an output may not be relied on for by itself.
Name the point at which a human must review or overturn an output.
Give the route for reporting odd or harmful behaviour during use.
Record which teams received the instructions and on what date.

title.en: Set responsible-use objectives and the thresholds that pause a system already in production

description.en: Say what good use of each live system looks like in numbers the operating team can read — override rate, complaint volume, accuracy on the population it actually sees, the share of outputs a human changed — and attach to each one a threshold that triggers a pause, a fallback to manual handling, or a referral back for reassessment. Objectives with no threshold produce a dashboard nobody acts on, and thresholds with no owner produce a breach everyone saw and nobody called. Attach the objective set with its thresholds and named owners.

evidenceHint.en: Objective set per live system: the measure, its threshold, the action taken on breach and the person who calls it

text.en: Choose the measures that show each system is being used well.
Attach a numeric threshold to every measure you keep.
State the action that follows a breach: pause, fallback or reassessment.
Name the person who declares a threshold breached.
Agree the objectives with the team that runs the system day to day.

title.en: Authorise every new use of a deployed system against the purpose it was originally assessed for

description.en: Run a standing gate: before an existing system is pointed at a new population, a new dataset, a new decision or a new market, someone checks the request against that system's assessed purpose and either authorises it, sends it back for a fresh impact assessment, or refuses it. The failure this prevents is quiet and cheap — a model bought for one job is reused for a second because it is already paid for and already integrated, and nobody re-ran the assessment because no new system was deployed. Keep one register row per request, refusals included.

evidenceHint.en: New-use decision register for the period: the request, the system, the outcome of the purpose check and any reassessment raised

text.en: Require a written request before a system is used for anything new.
Compare each request against that system's recorded purpose baseline.
Refer requests that go beyond it for a fresh impact assessment.
Log the decision, the reason and the date against every request.
Tell the requester the outcome and record who decided it.

title.en: Compare actual usage over the period with the approved purpose and the use objectives

description.en: Once a period, read what the systems were actually used for — usage logs, override records, support tickets and the new-use register — and put that beside the purpose baseline and the objective thresholds. Look specifically for uses that never passed the gate, because scope creep rarely arrives as a request: it arrives as a quietly widened integration, or as a team that found the API useful. For each departure, settle whether the use stops or is authorised with its assessment reworked. Attach the usage review with findings and decisions.

evidenceHint.en: Usage review for the period: measured objective results, undeclared uses found in the logs, and the stop-or-reassess decision against each

text.en: Pull usage logs and override records for each live system.
Measure each use objective against the threshold set for it.
Search the logs for uses that never appeared in the register.
Decide for each departure whether to stop it or reassess it.
Report the results to the owner accountable for the system.

templates.title: A.10 Third-party and customer relationships
templates.description: Implements AIMS-15: accountability for AI obligations is allocated across the supply chain, suppliers are held to stated AI expectations before and during use, and obligations arising from customer agreements are carried into the organisation's own AI approach (A.10.2-A.10.4).

title.en: Allocate each AI obligation across the supply chain to the party answerable for it

description.en: Take the AI systems in scope and decide, obligation by obligation, which party actually answers for it: the organisation, a supplier upstream, or the customer operating the output. The failure this prevents is mutual assumption — the supplier believes the deployer watches for drift, the deployer believes the supplier does, and nobody watches until an incident exposes the gap. Include the sub-suppliers a supplier itself depends on, because an obligation allocated to a party that has quietly outsourced it has not been allocated at all. Attach the matrix with every unclaimed obligation listed rather than silently dropped.

evidenceHint.en: Supply-chain accountability matrix: one row per externally supplied AI component, naming who answers for each obligation and listing the unclaimed gaps

text.en: Take the externally supplied AI components from the existing resource inventory.
Name the supplier behind each component and any sub-supplier it relies on.
Split each obligation — data quality, testing, monitoring, incident handling — between the parties.
Record every obligation where two parties each assume the other holds it.
Confirm the allocation with the named contact at the supplier and the customer.

title.en: Set the AI expectations a supplier must meet before its model or service is used in production

description.en: Write down what the organisation requires of an AI supplier and put it somewhere an agreement can reference, so it is a negotiating position rather than a discovery made after signature. Cover what the supplier must disclose about training data, evaluation results and known limitations, what it must report when a model version changes, and what the organisation is entitled to test or verify for itself. Mark which expectations cannot be traded away, because a schedule with no ranking gets conceded item by item in the last hour of a negotiation. Attach the schedule as it is referenced in agreements.

evidenceHint.en: Supplier AI requirements schedule, stating the disclosure, change-notification and verification terms attached to each expectation

text.en: Write the expectations into a schedule an agreement can reference directly.
State what the supplier must disclose about training data, evaluation and known limits.
Set what must be reported when the supplier changes a model version or endpoint.
Mark which expectations are non-negotiable and which may be traded in negotiation.
Agree the route by which the organisation may verify or test a supplier claim.

title.en: Map each obligation the customer agreements create onto the internal process that has to meet it

description.en: Go through the in-force customer agreements and pull out what they oblige the organisation to do about its AI — and what they oblige the customer to do in its own use of the output. Give each obligation an owning process and a named owner, and flag the ones no current process satisfies. An obligation that lives in a signed contract and in no process is one the organisation learns about when a customer asks for it, which is the worst moment to find out. This register records who owes what to whom; the content of any customer-facing documentation is a separate control's subject.

evidenceHint.en: Customer obligation register giving the clause, the party it binds, the owning process and owner, and the unsatisfied clauses flagged

text.en: Extract the AI-related clauses from every in-force customer agreement.
State what each clause obliges the organisation to do, and through which process.
Note the obligations the agreement places on the customer's own use of the output.
Name the owner for each obligation and where the evidence for it lands.
Flag any clause that no internal process currently satisfies.

title.en: Run the supplier AI check at onboarding and at renewal, and log every accepted shortfall

description.en: The recurring act: put the expectations schedule to the supplier, compare what comes back against it item by item, and record the outcome per engagement. Write down every shortfall that was accepted anyway, who accepted it and for how long — an accepted gap that is not recorded becomes indistinguishable from a gap nobody noticed. Repeat when the supplier materially changes the service, because a supplier assessed once at onboarding is being trusted against a product that may no longer exist. Attach the assessment file for each engagement in the period.

evidenceHint.en: Per-engagement supplier assessment file holding the answers received, the item-by-item comparison, and dated sign-off on each accepted deviation

text.en: Send the expectations schedule to the supplier before the agreement is signed.
Compare the answers received against each expectation, item by item.
Record every shortfall accepted, who accepted it and for how long.
Repeat the check at renewal or when the service materially changes.

title.en: Examine the incidents and complaints that crossed a supplier or customer boundary, and correct the allocation

description.en: The allocation's only honest test is what happened when something went wrong across an organisational boundary. For each case in the period, compare the party the matrix said was answerable with the party that actually dealt with it, and treat every mismatch as a defect in the allocation or in the agreement rather than as a one-off. Where a supplier or a customer declined an obligation the matrix assigned them, raise the amendment instead of leaving the matrix asserting something the parties have already refused. Attach the review with the amendments it produced.

evidenceHint.en: Boundary-incident review listing each case, the party named in the matrix, the party that acted, and the contract or allocation amendments raised

text.en: Collect the incidents, complaints and escalations that involved a supplier or customer.
Decide for each which party the allocation said was answerable.
Compare that against the party who in fact handled the case.
Raise a contract or allocation amendment wherever the two differ.
Carry the corrections into the accountability matrix in the same pass.
